title: Philemon
subtitle: Paul's Letter to Philemon - Key Notes, Cross-References, and Messianic Connections (WEB)

items.value: Philemon is a private letter about one man, carried home by the man it is about: a runaway slave named Onesimus, sent back to the master he wronged.
It is the most personal of Paul's letters, and the clearest picture in the New Testament of what it looks like when someone else pays your debt.

sections.heading: How this study is put together

items.value: Each of the shortest books in the Bible is one chapter long, so each one is a complete study in a single guide, laid out the same way as every other book in this series.

values: **Key Notes** - observations worth having in hand before you read, each ending with the verses it comes from.
**Key Cross-References** - passages that stand behind or alongside the text, grouped by theme.
**Messianic Connections** - places where the text reaches back into the Hebrew Scriptures or points ahead to the Messiah. Where an entry is a pattern rather than a prediction, the note says so.
**For Further Study** - places to go deeper.
**Introduction** - the book read as a whole before you read it in parts.
**The text itself**, printed in full in the World English Bible, with footnote markers on the verses the references belong to.

sections.heading: A note on the divine names

items.value: In the notes and introductions this study uses **Yahweh** for the covenant name of God and **Yahshua** for the Messiah. The printed scripture text is never altered; the World English Bible stands exactly as the translators set it, so our own speech and the translator's work stay visibly distinct.
Paul wrote it as a prisoner, traditionally in Rome, around the same time as Colossians, which names Onesimus and Archippus and was probably carried on the same journey.

Philemon, a believer in Colossae in whose house the assembly met. Apphia and Archippus, probably his household. Onesimus, his slave, who ran away, met Paul, and came to faith. And Paul's companions: Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke.

values: **Verses 1-7** - greeting, and thanks for the love that refreshes the saints.
**Verses 8-16** - the appeal for Onesimus, useless once and useful now, a brother rather than a slave.
**Verses 17-22** - receive him as you would receive me; put his debt to my account.

chapters.heading: PHILEMON - A Runaway Sent Home, Useless Made Useful, and Put It to My Account
chapters.title: A Runaway Sent Home, Useless Made Useful, and Put It to My Account
keyNotes: Paul writes as a prisoner, not an apostle. He opens no other letter that way. He is asking a favor as one bound man for another (Philemon 1:1, 1:9).
Philemon lived in Colossae. Paul's letter to the Colossians names Onesimus as one of you, and Archippus too, so the two letters likely traveled together (Philemon 1:2, Colossians 4:9, 4:17).
Apphia is often taken to be Philemon's wife, and Archippus their son, though the letter does not say so (Philemon 1:2).

"The assembly in your house." There were no church buildings. Believers met in homes, and this home belonged to the man whose slave had run away. The whole assembly would hear the letter read (Philemon 1:2, Romans 16:5).
"The hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you." Paul praises Philemon for the very quality he is about to ask him to use (Philemon 1:7, 1:20).

"Though I have all boldness in Christ to command you... for love's sake I rather beg." Paul has authority and lays it down. A forgiveness that is ordered is not really forgiveness (Philemon 1:8-9, 1:14).
"Paul, the aged" - or, by a change of one letter, Paul the ambassador. Either way he is leaning on who he is, not on what he could demand (Philemon 1:9).
"My child, whom I have become the father of in my chains." Onesimus came to faith through Paul while Paul was in prison. Chains did not stop the work (Philemon 1:10).
Onesimus means useful or profitable. Paul plays on it: once useless to you, now useful to you and to me. Grace made his name true (Philemon 1:11).
"I am sending him back... my own heart." Paul sends part of himself home in Onesimus (Philemon 1:12).

The Torah says: you shall not deliver to his master a servant who has escaped to you; let him live where he chooses, and do not oppress him. Paul does not hand Onesimus over against his will. Onesimus goes back with Paul's letter, to be received as a brother (Philemon 1:12, Deuteronomy 23:15-16).
"I desired to keep with me." Paul wanted him to stay and would not keep him without Philemon's consent. He would not do even a good thing by taking a choice away from someone else (Philemon 1:13-14).

"Perhaps he was therefore separated from you for a while, that you would have him forever." Joseph told his brothers: you meant it for evil, but God meant it for good. The wrong is not excused; it is redeemed (Philemon 1:15, Genesis 50:20).

"No longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother." The Torah forbade making a brother serve as a slave; he was to be as a hired worker and go free at the Jubilee. Paul applies that brotherhood to a man who was not born an Israelite (Philemon 1:16, Leviticus 25:39-42).
"Both in the flesh and in the Lord." A brother in the flesh - in ordinary daily life in that house - and a brother in the Lord. The change was meant to show (Philemon 1:16).
"If then you count me a partner, receive him as you would receive me." Paul asks Philemon to see Onesimus with Paul's face on him (Philemon 1:17).

"If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, put that to my account." Onesimus may have stolen when he ran. Paul takes the debt on himself. Isaiah: Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all (Philemon 1:18, Isaiah 53:6).

The Torah required restitution when a man had wronged another - the whole amount and a fifth more. Paul does not cancel the debt by pretending it is not there. He pays it (Philemon 1:18, Leviticus 6:4-5).

"I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it." A signed promissory note, in the middle of a letter. Paul usually dictated and signed at the end in his own hand (Philemon 1:19, Colossians 4:18).

"Not to mention to you that you owe to me even your own self." Philemon also came to faith through Paul. The man being asked to forgive a debt owes a far larger one himself - which is the point of the servant forgiven ten thousand talents (Philemon 1:19, Matthew 18:32-33).
"Refresh my heart in the Lord." The same word as verse 7. Paul asks Philemon to do for him what he has done for everyone else (Philemon 1:20, 1:7).
"You will do even beyond what I say." Some read a hint here that Paul hoped Philemon would set Onesimus free. The letter does not say it outright (Philemon 1:21).
"Prepare a guest room for me." Paul plans to come and see how it went. Forgiveness with a visit coming is forgiveness with accountability (Philemon 1:22).

Mark is named among Paul's fellow workers - the same Mark Paul refused to take on his second journey because he had deserted them. Paul knew about second chances. Later he wrote: bring Mark, for he is useful to me (Philemon 1:24, 2 Timothy 4:11).
Demas is here a fellow worker. In Paul's last letter Demas has left him, having loved this present world. Not every name in a greeting list finishes the race (Philemon 1:24, 2 Timothy 4:10).

A bishop named Onesimus led the assembly in Ephesus a few decades later, according to a letter of Ignatius. Whether he was the same man is not known, but some have thought so - and that he may have helped gather Paul's letters, including this one (Philemon 1:10).

intro: The letter concerns one man and was carried by him. Philemon, a believer of means in Colossae, in whose house the assembly met, owned a slave named Onesimus, who ran away, very likely taking something with him. In circumstances the letter does not describe, Onesimus came to Paul, then a prisoner, and came to faith through him. Paul, who calls him his own heart and would have liked to keep him, sends him home instead, bearing this letter to the master he had wronged.

Paul writes as a prisoner rather than an apostle and declines to command what he could command, because forgiveness on orders is not forgiveness. He plays on the slave's name - useful - once useless to Philemon and now useful to them both. He reads the whole episode as Joseph read his brothers' betrayal: perhaps Onesimus was parted for a while so that Philemon might have him forever, no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother, in daily life and in the Lord. The Torah had already forbidden making a brother serve as a slave, and Paul extends that brotherhood to a man not born an Israelite. Nor does he hand Onesimus over against his will; Onesimus returns with Paul's plea in his hand.

At the center of the letter is the request to receive Onesimus as Paul himself, and if he owes anything, to put it to Paul's account - the shape of Isaiah's servant on whom Yahweh laid the iniquity of us all. The debt is acknowledged and paid, not ignored. Paul signs the promise in his own hand, then gently reminds Philemon that he owes Paul his very self, the same reasoning as the parable of the servant forgiven ten thousand talents. He closes by asking for a guest room, since he means to come. We are not told how Philemon answered. The letter was kept, and a generation later the assembly in Ephesus had a leader named Onesimus.

verses.1: Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, to Philemon, our beloved fellow worker,
verses.2: to the beloved Apphia, to Archippus, our fellow soldier, and to the assembly in your house:
verses.3: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verses.4: I thank my God always, making mention of you in my prayers,
verses.5: hearing of your love, and of the faith which you have toward the Lord Jesus, and toward all the saints;
verses.6: that the fellowship of your faith may become effective, in the knowledge of every good thing which is in us in Christ Jesus.
verses.7: For we have much joy and comfort in your love, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you, brother.
verses.8: Therefore though I have all boldness in Christ to command you that which is appropriate,
verses.9: yet for love’s sake I rather beg, being such a one as Paul, the aged, but also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.
verses.10: I beg you for my child, whom I have become the father of in my chains, Onesimus,
verses.11: who once was useless to you, but now is useful to you and to me.
verses.12: I am sending him back. Therefore receive him, that is, my own heart,
verses.13: whom I desired to keep with me, that on your behalf he might serve me in my chains for the Good News.
verses.14: But I was willing to do nothing without your consent, that your goodness would not be as of necessity, but of free will.
verses.15: For perhaps he was therefore separated from you for a while, that you would have him forever,
verses.16: no longer as a slave, but more than a slave, a beloved brother, especially to me, but how much rather to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.
verses.17: If then you count me a partner, receive him as you would receive me.
verses.18: But if he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, put that to my account.
verses.19: I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it (not to mention to you that you owe to me even your own self besides).
verses.20: Yes, brother, let me have joy from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in the Lord.
verses.21: Having confidence in your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even beyond what I say.
verses.22: Also, prepare a guest room for me, for I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you.
verses.23: Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you,
verses.24: as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers.
verses.25: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.

cites.text: Greet the assembly that is in their house. Greet Epaenetus, my beloved, who is the first fruits of Achaia to Christ.
Greet the brothers who are in Laodicea, and Nymphas, and the assembly that is in his house.

2.why: the assembly that is in their house, and Nymphas and the assembly in his house

cites.text: together with Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you. They will make known to you everything that is going on here.

10.why: Onesimus, the faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you

cites.text: You shall not deliver to his master a servant who has escaped from his master to you. He shall dwell with you, among you, in the place which he shall choose within one of your gates, where it pleases him best. You shall not oppress him.

12.why: do not deliver to his master a servant who has escaped to you, and do not oppress him

cites.text: As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is today, to save many people alive.
Now don’t be grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life.

15.why: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, and God sent me before you to preserve life

cites.text: “‘If your brother has grown poor among you, and sells himself to you; you shall not make him to serve as a slave. As a hired servant, and as a temporary resident, he shall be with you; he shall serve with you until the Year of Jubilee: then he shall go out from you, he and his children with him, and shall return to his own family, and to the possession of his fathers. For they are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt. They shall not be sold as slaves.
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.

16.why: your brother shall not serve as a slave but go free at the Jubilee, and neither slave nor free, all one

cites.text: You shall make the fiftieth year holy, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee to you; and each of you shall return to his own property, and each of you shall return to his family.

The Lord Yahweh’s Spirit is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;

16.why: liberty proclaimed throughout the land, and the anointed one sent to proclaim liberty to the captives

cites.text: All we like sheep have gone astray. Everyone has turned to his own way; and Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all.
After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities.

18.why: Yahweh has laid on him the iniquity of us all, and he will bear their iniquities

cites.text: then it shall be, if he has sinned, and is guilty, he shall restore that which he took by robbery, or the thing which he has gotten by oppression, or the deposit which was committed to him, or the lost thing which he found, or any thing about which he has sworn falsely; he shall restore it even in full, and shall add a fifth part more to it. He shall return it to him to whom it belongs in the day of his being found guilty.
then he shall confess his sin which he has done, and he shall make restitution for his guilt in full, and add to it the fifth part of it, and give it to him in respect of whom he has been guilty.

18.why: restore what was taken in full and add a fifth, and make restitution for the guilt

cites.text: “‘If an alien or temporary resident with you becomes rich, and your brother beside him has grown poor, and sells himself to the stranger or foreigner living among you, or to a member of the stranger’s family; after he is sold he may be redeemed. One of his brothers may redeem him; or his uncle, or his uncle’s son, may redeem him, or any who is a close relative to him of his family may redeem him; or if he has grown rich, he may redeem himself.

Boaz said to the elders, and to all the people, “You are witnesses today, that I have bought all that was Elimelech’s, and all that was Chilion’s and Mahlon’s, from the hand of Naomi. Moreover Ruth the Moabitess, the wife of Mahlon, I have purchased to be my wife, to raise up the name of the dead on his inheritance, that the name of the dead may not be cut off from among his brothers, and from the gate of his place. You are witnesses today.”

19.why: a brother or close relative may redeem him, and Boaz redeeming what was Elimelech's before witnesses

cites.text: See with what large letters I write to you with my own hand.
The salutation of me, Paul, with my own hand: remember my bonds. Grace be with you. Amen.

19.why: large letters written with my own hand, and the greeting of Paul with my own hand

cites.text: For I have satiated the weary soul, and I have replenished every sorrowful soul.”
He restores my soul. He guides me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake.

20.why: I have satiated the weary soul, and he restores my soul

cites.text: Aristarchus, my fellow prisoner, greets you, and Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (concerning whom you received commandments, “if he comes to you, receive him”), and Jesus who is called Justus. These are my only fellow workers for God’s Kingdom who are of the circumcision, men who have been a comfort to me. Epaphras, who is one of you, a servant of Christ, salutes you, always striving for you in his prayers, that you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God. For I testify about him, that he has great zeal for you, and for those in Laodicea, and for those in Hierapolis. Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas greet you.

for Demas left me, having loved this present world, and went to Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for service.

24.why: Mark, Luke and Demas greeting the Colossians, and Demas leaving while Mark is useful for service

parts.title: Major Themes in Philemon
items: A letter carried by the man it was about
A prisoner asking, when he could command
Forgiveness that must be chosen to be real
Chains that did not stop a new birth
Useless made useful, and a name made true
Sent home to the one he wronged
Not handed over, but sent with a plea
Parted for a while to be received forever
What was meant for evil, meant by God for good
No longer a slave, but a brother in the flesh and in the Lord
Received with someone else's face on him
Put it to my account: the debt acknowledged and paid
A promise signed in his own hand
The forgiver who owes a greater debt
Mark, who got a second chance, and Demas, who did not finish
